Hands-on AI test · everyday office work

I gave three AI assistants a normal day of office work. Only one could run it end to end.

Not a coding contest. The ordinary jobs a non-technical business user actually does: build the deck, clean the messy spreadsheet, draft the emails, find a slot in the calendar. Run through Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft 365 Copilot, then graded blind.

By Michael Mortensen, SpAIke · ~7 min read

Most AI comparisons are about coding, maths or deep research. Fascinating if you are an engineer. Beside the point if you are a commercial lead who just needs the board deck built, the sales sheet cleaned up, the follow-up emails drafted and a meeting slotted into the week. So I tested the part that actually fills a normal workday.

The focus here is deliberately un-technical: the everyday knowledge work a business person does inside files, email and calendar. Not "how well does it code," but "how well does it support you in the job you already have." I gave three assistants one realistic project, launching a Danish oat-milk cold brew, with nine ordinary deliverables from a single brief:

  • Turn raw research notes into a one-page market brief
  • Clean a messy sales spreadsheet (duplicates, a wrong total, a returns row, blanks)
  • Build a three-year forecast
  • Audit a P&L that has three mistakes hidden in it on purpose
  • Write a formatted board report with a clear recommendation
  • Build a pitch deck with speaker notes
  • Generate a product image
  • Write a go-to-market plan that respects a fixed budget and rules
  • Find the launch-review email, propose a time, and put a tentative hold in the calendar

Same inputs, three contestants: Claude (in its file-aware Cowork mode), ChatGPT, and Microsoft 365 Copilot. This is the kind of work where you hand over your files and expect a finished result, not a chat.

How I kept the scoring honest

One person's opinion on nine deliverables is just taste. So I anonymised every output into Set A, B and C, stripped the fingerprints, and had three fresh sessions of Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot grade all three sets blind, with no idea which tool made what. The result held up: the three judges broadly agreed, and where a judge did nudge its own set up, it was mild, one judge was actually hardest on a rival rather than on itself. So the numbers below are not just my preference. A plain script also checked the hard facts: did the maths tie out, did the cleaned data hit the right totals, did each tool catch the planted spreadsheet errors.

Claude and ChatGPT finished essentially tied at the top; Copilot came a clear third. But the ranking is the least interesting part. Three things underneath it matter more for how you would actually use these tools day to day.

1. All three can now actually do the work

A year ago a job like this needed constant hand-holding. Not anymore. Every one of the three produced a board-ready deck, a cleaned-up spreadsheet, a real go-to-market plan and a usable product image. More telling for everyday use: I had hidden three mistakes in the P&L, a total that silently skipped a cost line, a profit margin typed in wrong, and two figures swapped. All three found all three. That is the quietly important part. These assistants are now good enough to catch the error buried in your own data, not just generate new text on top of it. The floor has moved, and for most everyday office work it is now high.

2. Copilot is better than its reputation

If your real question is "has Copilot become good enough," the honest answer on quality is largely yes. One of the eight things I scored was autonomy: could it take the whole job from one instruction and run it across files, mail and calendar. Set that single axis aside and score only the quality of the finished work, and the gap narrows sharply.

ToolOverall /40Quality only /35Quality %Autonomy /5
Claude37.332.392%5.0
ChatGPT37.032.392%4.7
Copilot26.725.071%1.7

Set autonomy aside and Claude and ChatGPT are dead even on quality, both at 92%; Copilot sits at 71%. Copilot's gap is nearly all on that one axis, not in the craft of any single document. Its go-to-market plan scored level with the others, and its deck and product image were genuinely good. This is not a weak tool. It is a strong tool with one specific limit.

3. The real difference is how much you carry

This is the finding that matters most for a normal working day. With Claude I dropped in every file, of every type, and said "go." One door. It read the spreadsheet, cleaned it, built the forecast, caught a mistake of its own on a second pass, wrote the report, made the deck, generated the image, drafted the email and put a tentative hold on my calendar. One instruction, one finished pack.

Copilot made me walk into Excel for the spreadsheet, then into PowerPoint for the deck, then into Word for the document, one task at a time, room by room. There is no single front door where you say "build the launch pack" and it gathers what it needs. Its attempt to run the whole job from one prompt did not finish.

It is not that Copilot works badly. It is that you are still the one carrying the work from room to room.

For a non-technical user, that is the whole game. You do not want to become the project manager for your own assistant. You want to hand over the task and get the result.

Credit where it is due: Copilot

Third place makes Copilot easy to write off, and that would be a mistake. It caught all three planted spreadsheet errors, exactly like the other two. Its go-to-market plan scored on par with ChatGPT and near Claude. Its product image and deck were genuinely good, and it produces native, editable Office files right where you already work. It computes correctly and makes solid documents. Its limit is orchestration, not craft.

Why I did not test Copilot Cowork

Copilot does have a dedicated agentic mode, Cowork, that would put it on equal footing with Claude's Cowork and ChatGPT's Work. I deliberately did not test it, for three honest reasons.

1. Under the hood, Cowork runs the same frontier models, Claude and GPT. Point it at Claude and you get essentially Claude's quality, so a test would mostly re-measure a model I had already scored. It would be Claude grading Claude.

2. Almost nobody actually has it yet. Cowork is sold on usage-based billing only: metered Copilot Credits on top of a paid Copilot licence, an admin has to wire up Azure pay-as-you-go, and access is gated on rollout. I hold the licence and set the billing up myself, and a day later it still had not unlocked. In most organisations, few users will get IT to switch on open-ended, pay-per-task spend.

3. So the useful question for the people who actually use Copilot today, on the ordinary, non-agentic chat, is simple: what does that version do, and what does it cost? That is exactly what these scores measure.

The pricing contrast is worth seeing plainly, because it is the real adoption barrier:

ToolAgentic modeHow you pay for it
ClaudeCoworkIncluded in the flat subscription, with fair-use limits
ChatGPTWorkIncluded in the flat subscription, with fair-use limits
CopilotCoworkMetered per task (Copilot Credits), on top of a paid licence, plus admin setup

With Claude and ChatGPT you just say "go." With Copilot, every task carries a price, an admin has to switch on pay-as-you-go, and the default spend cap is so low you cannot run even one heavy task without raising it. For a non-technical user or a small business, that is real friction, and a running "can I afford to run this one?" question.

What I am not claiming

  • This is one realistic scenario, not a full suite. A deliberately messy job, but a sample of one.
  • It is a snapshot of August 2026, not a trend. These tools change every month.
  • The judges are the same kind of model being judged. The blind design and the self-preference check exist precisely to keep that honest, and I spot-checked by hand too.

So which one should you use?

If your work lives inside Microsoft 365 and you are happy to drive it program by program, Copilot earns its seat. It is genuinely capable inside each app. If you would rather hand one assistant the whole messy task, of mixed file types, and have it come back with a finished result while you get on with your day, that is a different job, and right now it has a clear leader.

The useful question was never which AI is smartest. It is which one actually takes the work off your desk.

This is the kind of test I run for a living.
